raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic systolic heart failure syndrome presenting toward the end of pregnancy or, more commonly, in the months after delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause. The modern definition emphasizes left ventricular systolic dysfunction, usually left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45%, rather than a strict time window, because some women present late or have unrecognized antenatal disease [1-6]. PPCM is clinically important because it affects otherwise young women, may deteriorate rapidly, and has implications for breastfeeding, contraception, and future pregnancy.

Reported incidence varies widely by geography and ascertainment. Population-based North American studies suggest approximately 1 case per 1,000–4,000 live births, with increasing recognition over time [7-11]. Higher rates have been reported in women of African ancestry and in regions with high burdens of hypertensive pregnancy disorders, multiparity, nutritional stress, or limited access to care [7-13]. Risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiple gestation, pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, Black race, multiparity, and assisted reproduction; however, many affected women lack obvious risk factors [8-14]. Contemporary prospective cohorts show that early diagnosis, baseline LVEF, left ventricular size, right ventricular involvement, and access to guideline-directed heart failure therapy strongly influence recovery [12-14].

The pathobiology is multifactorial. Earlier hypotheses emphasized myocarditis, maladaptive inflammation, and autoimmunity; inflammatory markers have been associated with worse outcomes in prospective cohorts [15,23]. A central mechanistic model links late-pregnancy oxidative stress with cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic and proapoptotic fragment, causing endothelial and myocardial injury [17]. Angiogenic imbalance also appears important: excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1, common in pre-eclampsia and multiple gestation, may impair vascular homeostasis and help explain the association between PPCM and hypertensive pregnancy disorders [16,18]. MicroRNA-146a has been proposed as both mediator and biomarker in prolactin-fragment signaling [19]. Genetics increasingly bridges PPCM and dilated cardiomyopathy: truncating variants, particularly in TTN, are enriched in PPCM and predict lower likelihood of recovery in some series [20-22]. Thus PPCM is best viewed as a pregnancy-triggered cardiomyopathy in susceptible myocardium rather than a single disease.

Presentation resembles other forms of heart failure but overlaps with normal pregnancy symptoms. Dyspnea, orthopnea, cough, edema, fatigue, palpitations, chest discomfort, thromboembolism, or cardiogenic shock may occur. Evaluation should include electrocardiography, natriuretic peptides, chest imaging when indicated, and transthoracic echocardiography to assess LVEF, ventricular size, right ventricular function, valvular disease, pulmonary pressures, and intracardiac thrombus [3-6]. Cardiac magnetic resonance can help exclude alternative diagnoses, characterize tissue, and quantify function, although gadolinium is generally avoided during pregnancy unless essential. Differential diagnoses include pre-existing dilated cardiomyopathy, congenital or valvular disease, ischemia or spontaneous coronary artery dissection, pulmonary embolism, myocarditis, sepsis-related cardiomyopathy, and hypertensive pulmonary edema.

Management depends on pregnancy status and severity. During pregnancy, fetal-safe heart failure therapy includes loop diuretics for congestion, beta-blockers, hydralazine–nitrate combinations, digoxin, and anticoagulation when indicated; angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are generally avoided until after delivery [3,4,30]. Delivery is indicated for obstetric reasons or maternal instability; vaginal delivery with careful anesthesia and hemodynamic monitoring is preferred when stable. Postpartum, standard heart failure therapy should be introduced and uptitrated, while considering lactation safety and maternal preference [3,4,30]. Anticoagulation is often considered when LVEF is severely reduced, particularly <30–35%, or when atrial fibrillation, ventricular thrombus, or bromocriptine use is present.

Bromocriptine, which suppresses prolactin, is biologically attractive. A South African pilot trial and a German randomized study suggested improved recovery with bromocriptine added to heart failure therapy, but sample sizes were modest and anticoagulation is required because of thrombotic risk [24,25]. Consequently, bromocriptine is used variably and is most often considered for severe presentations in experienced centers. Arrhythmic risk is highest early in women with markedly reduced LVEF; a wearable defibrillator may provide temporary protection while awaiting recovery, whereas permanent implantable defibrillators are usually deferred for at least 3–6 months unless standard indications persist [26].

Prognosis is heterogeneous. Many women recover LVEF within 6–12 months, especially when baseline LVEF is >30%, left ventricular dilation is limited, and therapy is prompt [12-14]. Others progress to chronic heart failure, require mechanical circulatory support or transplantation, or die. Counseling after recovery is essential. Subsequent pregnancy carries relapse risk even when LVEF normalizes, and risk is substantially higher when systolic dysfunction persists [27-29]. Women with persistent LVEF <50% are generally advised to avoid pregnancy; those with recovered function require individualized counseling, preconception imaging, medication review, close cardio-obstetric surveillance, and rapid postpartum follow-up.
